title: The Emin Pasha Relief Expedition
intro: Henry Morton Stanley led a force of nearly 700 men across Africa to relieve Emin Pasha, the besieged Egyptian governor of Equatoria. The route ran by sea round the Cape to the Congo, up the river, through the Ituri rainforest to Lake Albert, and out to the east coast.
ending: The expedition reached Bagamoyo on 4 December. Stanley was first acclaimed, but criticism followed as the deaths of so many of its members and reports of brutality became known.

legs.title: By sea round Africa to the Congo

stops.text: Stanley arrived from London. Egyptian objections to the Congo route were overridden by a telegram from Lord Salisbury, and the expedition was allowed to march under the Egyptian flag.
stops.quote: Stanley departed London on 21 January 1887 and arrived in Cairo on 27 January. Egyptian objections to the Congo route were overridden by a telegram from Lord Salisbury, and the expedition was permitted to march under the Egyptian flag.

stops.text: Stanley arrived and made two agreements with Tippu Tib, one appointing him Governor of Stanley Falls, which was much criticised in Europe as a deal with a slave-trader, and one for carriers.
stops.quote: Stanley left Cairo on 3 February, joined up with expedition members during stops in Suez and Aden, and arrived in Zanzibar on 22 February.

stops.text: The expedition left Zanzibar on 25 February and sailed round the Cape of Good Hope towards the mouth of the Congo.
stops.quote: The expedition left Zanzibar on 25 February and, rounding the Cape of Good Hope, arrived at Banana at the mouth of the Congo on 18 March.

stops.wp: Banana, Democratic Republic of the Congo
stops.text: The expedition arrived at the mouth of the Congo somewhat unexpectedly, because a broken telegraph cable had left local officials without instructions.
stops.quote: arrived at Banana at the mouth of the Congo on 18 March. Their arrival was somewhat unexpected, because a telegraph cable had broken and local officials had received no instructions.

stops.text: Chartered steamers brought the expedition to Matadi. There the carriers took over, bringing some 800 loads of stores and ammunition overland, slowly, in the rainy season and with food short.
stops.quote: Chartered steamers brought the expedition to Matadi, where the carriers took over, bringing some 800 loads of stores and ammunition to Leopoldville on the Stanley Pool.

stops.text: Of the steamers King Leopold had promised, only one worked. Stanley requisitioned two from missionaries, overriding their protests, left many stores behind, and announced a rear column and an Advance Column.
stops.quote: On 21 April, the expedition arrived at Leopoldville. King Leopold had promised a flotilla of river steamers, but only one worked: the Stanley.

legs.title: Up the Congo and through the Ituri forest

stops.text: The villagers refused permission to stay, so Stanley attacked, drove them away and made the village a fortified camp. The rear column was left here, and Stanley set out for Lake Albert on 28 June.
stops.quote: The inhabitants of Yambuya refused permission to reside in their village, so Stanley attacked and drove the villagers away, turning the deserted village into a fortified camp.

stops.text: Stanley found Bonny, the only European left with the rear column, and a handful of starving carriers. Barttelot had been shot in a dispute, and Jameson was at Bangala dying of a fever.
stops.quote: Finally, on 17 August at Banalya, 90 miles upstream from Yambuya, Stanley found Bonny, the sole European left in charge of the column, along with a handful of starving carriers.

stops.text: Commissioner Wissmann met the expedition and escorted it into Bagamoyo. The Zanzibari carriers were paid off or, if prisoners, returned to their masters, and the Sudanese and Egyptians were sent back to Egypt.
stops.quote: were met by commissioner Wissmann on 4 December and escorted into Bagamoyo.

notes: Years are inferred from the surrounding narrative where the article gives only day and month (Zanzibar, Banana, Leopoldville, Banalya, Fort Bodo, Usambiro, Bagamoyo). Stops without a date in the article have null date and year (Cape, Matadi, Yambuya, Ibwiri). Left out: Ugarrowwa's and Ipoto (no dates or events beyond swapping equipment for food; no sure Wikipedia article), Bangala Station, Stanley Falls, Mswa, Dufile and Kavalli's (no dependable article title). Contradiction: the article says Jephson met Emin on 29 April 1888 and also that Emin met Stanley on the 29th, yet gives 18 April for Emin's letter. Ibwiri is a guess for Fort Bodo's point; Banalya is spelt Banalia on Wikipedia, check it is the same place. Zanzibar entry null: places.tsv has none.
